implementation_notes: Scala inherits the JVM monitor: AnyRef.synchronized executes a block with an exclusive lock on the receiver and releases it on every exit path, so the acquire/release pair disappears into the language, and a private lock object keeps it out of reach of other code. Timed or interruptible acquisition uses the java.util.concurrent locks behind the same block shape - Scala has no try-with-resources, so a small by-name helper (or an explicit try/finally) wraps them. That said, the idiomatic Scala treatment of shared mutable state is to remove the lock: immutable data, actor ownership, or the STM variant below.
pitfalls: synchronized on this or on any shared object exposes the monitor and can deadlock with unrelated code; use a private lock instance, and keep one lock per invariant.
It is thread-blocking and does not compose with Future or cats-effect/ZIO: blocking inside an execution context starves the pool, so such code should be pushed to a dedicated blocking context.
A helper that wraps java.util.concurrent locks around a by-name parameter reintroduces the explicit unlock inside the helper; bypassing the helper restores the forgotten-unlock failure mode.

variants.name: software transactional memory (ScalaSTM atomic blocks)
variants.implementation_notes: The concurrent-functional route: with ScalaSTM, atomic runs a block that reads and writes Refs as a transaction, and the runtime manages the locks, the commit and the retry loop - the programmer acquires nothing, and nested atomic blocks compose into one transaction instead of deadlocking. Choose it for in-memory shared state that is read-mostly and retried cheaply; the pessimistic synchronized variant remains the right tool when the protected resource is external (a connection, a file) and cannot participate in a transaction.
variants.code_sketch:
import scala.concurrent.stm._

val balance = Ref(0L)

def transfer(cents: Long): Unit = atomic { implicit txn =>
  balance += cents            // commit or retry handled by the STM runtime
}
pitfalls: Side effects inside atomic (I/O, logging, sending messages) run again on retry; keep transactions pure or move side effects to after-commit hooks.
Only Refs are protected: ordinary mutable state touched inside the block is outside the transaction, and a Ref read outside atomic is a compile error.
STM retries burn CPU under contention and cannot wrap blocking calls; long transactions are as harmful here as long lock holds.
